Hi Everyone!

Thanks so much for a wonderful class yesterday, and for a good start to our 6 weeks together. 

A bit of recap from yesterday's class:

(1) The tutorials we will be following are here:
https://www.qgistutorials.com/en/

Yesterday we did this:
- Making a Map (https://www.qgistutorials.com/en/docs/3/making_a_map.html)
- Working with Attributes (https://www.qgistutorials.com/en/docs/3/working_with_attributes.html)
- Check out the Taiwan Online Map Service (https://maps.nlsc.gov.tw/T09E/mapshow.action)

Remember to connect the QGIS program with the Taiwan Map Server by using the WMTS service -- pic below:

(2) Your homework for Tuesday at 1pm -- you have three things due:

a-> Please work through the two tutorials here:
"Basic Vector Styling" (https://www.qgistutorials.com/en/docs/3/basic_vector_styling.html
and
"Basic Raster Styling" (https://www.qgistutorials.com/en/docs/3/raster_styling_and_analysis.html)

The tutorials tell you exactly how to use the data that they give you, don't worry. 

b-> Please assemble a map with ONE raster layer and FOUR vector layers
- The map should be about Taiwan and hopefully about your project
- The map should be with data from the Taiwan map server (above)
- You should give your map a title, add a North arrow, and a scale grid
- You should export your map as a PDF with your name on it, and submit to this Discord channel
- Please don't submit anything except a PDF -- so, no PNG/JPG/GIF/etc

c-> (new) Please prepare a 5-6 minute presentation about your current science project.

(3) On Tuesday, we will meet for three hours, and the schedule will be as follows:
a) Learn more GIS techniques inside QGIS, including how to work with terrain data, raster and vector data
b) Check your homework and answer any questions
c) Present where you are in your current project. 

SO -- it's important that in addition to your homework, you come prepared to talk for 5-6 minutes about your project, and how you want to use GIS as a tool. 

I can't wait to see you all next week!

週末愉快！

Dr. Daniel

Timmy came across a study this week that's worth stealing a technique from. Researchers looked at 60 years of MLB data and found that warmer, thinner air from climate change accounted for ~1% of home runs (2010–2019), projected to rise toward 10% by 2100. The reason it's a compelling story isn't "climate is bad" — it's that something everyone attributed to human factors (strength, skill, steroids) turned out to be quietly shaped by an invisible variable (air density) all along.

messages.content: The text so far -- please finish editing for Monday, 7pm (final version):

Taiwan, barely 400 km long, holds both a tropical climate and a subtropical one at the same zone. The journey from Kaohsiung to Yushan, which takes approximately three hours by car, traverses a temperature greater than that between Miami and Anchorage, Alaska, with a of __ °C. This variation has significance way beyond simple weather fluctuations. The presence of two highly distinct climates within just 200 kilometers of land means that it can be incredibly hard to generalize knowledge and create a cohesive narrative about what Taiwan is. This is what topographical variation means: in most countries, climate changes gradually across hundreds of kilometers. In Taiwan, it can change by double digits within the space of a single county. 
Aside from large regional variations in temperature that can occur across Taiwan as one travels from North to South, over the past decades, Taiwan’s average temperature has also risen significantly. To put things into perspective: over the past 3 decades, Taiwan’s climate did not just warm up, the rate at which it is changing also sped up. For nearly a century, our island’s temperature crept upward by about 0.11 degrees Celsius every ten years, a pace so slow that a farmer could spend an entire career barely noticing it. In Taiwan, flat plains can allow for rice to thrive, while tea plants thrive in high mountains only an hour away. 
However, since 1991, this rate has almost tripled, to 0.29 degrees Celsius per decade. Notably, 2024 became the hottest year Taiwan has ever recorded, and Taipei alone logged 63 days above 35 degrees Celsius – nearly twenty more scorching days than the historical norm. To understand how the aforementioned acceleration is felt on the ground: in an average year, Kaohsiung’s lowland rice fields sit at a scorching 29.1 degrees Celsius, while Yushan’s alpine terraces (barely 200 km away) hover near a wintry 10.2, dipping below freezing in January.

The acceleration of climate change in Taiwan in parallel to the dire regional variations is exactly why Taiwanese agricultural knowledge was never uniform. Instead, it was built upon thousands of hyper-specific inherited bits of wisdom. In a situation where rising temperature is combined with, for example, an increase in soil salinity, small-scale farmers across Taiwan often do not have the luxury to exchange farming expertise with one another. 
The people most affected by climate change are also usually the oldest. The average Taiwanese farmer is 63.5 years old, and more than half of all farmers are over 65. This isn’t a workforce with decades left to retrain, relocate, and rebuild after a disaster. Among these communities, alpine farmers are the most vulnerable. As global warming increases the average temperature on low-land, cooler-climate plants move further up the mountain, slowly encroaching on other plants. This subtle encroachment means alpine farmers no longer have any higher, cooler ground left to retreat to anymore.
 In the face of shifting weather patterns, farmers have persevered so far with centuries of experience and wisdom. However, in the past decades, climate unpredictability has led to a gap between how fast tradition can adapt and how fast the climate is now moving. This is exactly where biomanufacturing belongs: not replacing what farmers know, but giving them a modern tool built to move at the same speed as the problem.
It impacts the alpine farmers as the rising temperatures cause cooler-climate plants to move further up the mountain, thus reducing the space for the plants to grow.
